subject: Boethius (Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius), honoured at Pavia as St Severinus Boethius

text_used.text: Quotations of the Consolation are checked word for word against H. R. James's translation (London, Elliot Stock, 1897), Project Gutenberg eBook 14328, downloaded whole as plain text (raw-gutenberg-14328-james.txt) and cut into one file per prose section and poem (james-b<book>-prose<n>.txt, james-b<book>-song<n>.txt). James numbers the prose sections as chapters and the poems as 'Songs'; modern editions say 'prose' and 'metre' (or 'poem'): James's Book II, chapter IV is Book II, prose 4. The Theological Tractates are checked against H. F. Stewart and E. K. Rand's Loeb translation (1918), Project Gutenberg eBook 13316 (Latin and English), and against CCEL's chapter pages of the same Loeb translation (ccel-tracts-iv.*.txt). The Latin of both works is the Loeb text in the same Gutenberg file. 'exact' is the translation as printed, footnote marks and underscores (italics) taken out. 'display' applies the site's capitals for every pronoun for God, where it differs. 'vol' is the whole-work file and 'page' the section file; both must contain the line.
text_used.source: Project Gutenberg 14328 (James) and 13316 (Stewart and Rand); CCEL, The Theological Tractates (Loeb 1918, marked Public Domain)
text_used.note: Links for Consolation lines go to Gutenberg's HTML copy of James with the printed page anchor (#Page_N) where the line stands. Wikisource has James split by poem; 25 of those pages were fetched (ws-james-*.txt) before Wikimedia rate-limited the fetch, so they are not used as links. CCEL's Consolation is a different translation (W. V. Cooper, 1902). The quiz's Consolation lines are James's words, not Cooper's. The whole Consolation is a dialogue: the prisoner 'Boethius' complains, and Lady Philosophy answers. Each line below says who speaks.

name.text: Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius. The 1883 decree and the Latin title in some copies add Torquatus. The king's letters spell him Boetius, and so does Procopius.
name.source: Stewart and Rand, Loeb 1918, title of On the Trinity ('A TREATISE BY ANICIUS MANLIUS SEVERINUS BOETHIUS'); Acta Sanctae Sedis 16 (1883), p. 302 ('Anicius Manlius Torquatus Severinus Boetius'); Hodgkin, Letters of Cassiodorus, note 223 ('spelt Boetius in the Variae'); Procopius, Wars 5.1.32 ('his son-in-law Boetius')
name.note: The Loeb's Latin heading gives his titles as the manuscripts do: 'ANICII MANLII SEVERINI BOETHII V.C. ET INL. EXCONS. ORD. EX MAG. OFF. PATRICII' (a man of the highest rank, ex-consul, ex-Master of Offices, patrician).

born.text: About 480, at Rome. Some put it a few years earlier (475 to 477).
born.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), 'Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius' ('born at Rome in 480'); Stewart and Rand, Introduction ('born about 480 A.D. in Rome'); Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya), 'Boethius' ('ок. 480, Рим'); Merriam-Webster ('circa 480–524'); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Boethius' (J. Marenbon, rev. 2021: 'born: circa 475–7 C.E.')
born.note: Hodgkin (Letters of Cassiodorus, 1886) explains the usual date: the 'untimely gray hairs' of Consolation Book 1 and hints in Ennodius 'entitle us to fix it at about 480, certainly not earlier than that year'. No ancient source gives the year.

family.text: From the old Roman family of the Anicii. His father, also a Boethius, was consul in 487 and died when he was a child.
family.source: Stewart and Rand, Introduction ('of the famous Praenestine family of the Anicii ... His father was an ex-consul'); Hodgkin ('The death of his father (who was Consul in 487) occurred while he was still a child'); Orthodox Encyclopedia (father Flavius Manlius, consul 487)
family.note: James's frontispiece is a consular ivory at Brescia showing 'Narius Manlius Boethius', which James takes to be the philosopher's father (James, Preface). The Orthodox Encyclopedia's caption says 'probably' the father.

grew_up.text: An orphan, raised in the house of Symmachus, a senator of great learning. He later married Symmachus's daughter Rusticiana.
grew_up.source: Consolation, Book 2, prose 3 (Philosophy: 'when orphaned and desolate, thou wast taken into the care of illustrious men'); Catholic Encyclopedia ('left an orphan at an early age and was educated by the pious and noble-minded Symmachus, whose daughter, Rusticana, he married'); James, Proem ('His parents dying early, he was brought up by Symmachus')
grew_up.exact: when orphaned and desolate, thou wast taken into the care of illustrious men
grew_up.note: The Catholic Encyclopedia prints 'Rusticana'; James and Procopius have 'Rusticiana'.

died.text: Put to death in 524, or perhaps 526, near Pavia in northern Italy, on the orders of King Theodoric. He was tortured with a cord tied round his forehead, then beaten to death with a club.
died.source: Anonymus Valesianus, part 2, section 87 (tr. J. C. Rolfe, Loeb 1939, LacusCurtius); Catholic Encyclopedia ('died at Pavia in 524 or 525'); Stewart and Rand ('brutally put to death in 524'); Orthodox Encyclopedia (524 by the dating of the 6th-century chronicler Marius of Avenches, or 526 by modern scholars); SEP ('probably in 526')
died.exact: He was tortured for a long time with a cord bound about his forehead so tightly that his eyes cracked in their sockets, and finally, while under torture, he was beaten to death with a cudgel.
died.latin: Qui accepta chorda in fronte diutissime tortus, ita ut oculi eius creparent, sic sub tormenta ad ultimum cum fuste occiditur.
died.note: No ancient source gives the day. Pavia keeps 23 October; Vatican News (Italian) says he was executed on 23 October 524, without a source. Hodgkin: 'execution (probably in the early part of 524)'. The place, 'the Calventian estate' (ager Calventianus), is usually taken to be Calvenzano, about 15 km north-east of Pavia (Thayer's note to Rolfe, following Muratori). Rolfe's own note 77 says the death sentence had first been changed to exile.

buried.text: At Pavia, in the church of San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro (St Peter in the Golden Sky), where the bones of St Augustine also lie. His tomb is in the crypt.
buried.source: Acta Sanctae Sedis 16 (1883), p. 303 (the citizens of Pavia moved his body into the basilica of St Peter 'ad caelum aureum'); Dante, Paradiso, Canto 10 (Longfellow: 'The body whence 'twas hunted forth is lying / Down in Cieldauro'); Basilica di San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro, 'San Severino Boezio' (2010: 'Le reliquie di San Severino Boezio nella cripta'); Orthodox Encyclopedia (his remains moved there in 721 by the Lombard king Liutprand, 'where the relics of Blessed Augustine also rest')
buried.exact: Down in Cieldauro, and from martyrdom And banishment it came unto this peace.
buried.note: The sources differ on when he was moved there: the 1883 decree says the citizens moved him soon after Theodoric died (526); the Orthodox Encyclopedia says 721. Gibbon (ch. 39) adds that the emperor Otto III 'removed to a more honorable tomb the bones' (about 1000). Say only 'buried at Pavia, in San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro'.

also_called.text: St Severinus Boethius (Italian: San Severino Boezio) at Pavia and in the Roman Martyrology. 'The last of the Romans', after Gibbon.
also_called.source: Roman Martyrology, 23 October, as quoted by Cathopedia and santodelgiorno.it ('A Pavia, commemorazione di san Severino Boezio, martire'); Acta Sanctae Sedis 16 (1883) ('SEVERINO BOETIO, philosopho martyri sancto nuncupato'); Catholic Encyclopedia ('often styled "the last of the Romans"')
also_called.note: The Orthodox Church has no name or title for him (see status).

status.text: Catholic: a saint and martyr with a local cult at Pavia, confirmed on 15 December 1883, and listed in the Roman Martyrology on 23 October. He is not in the General Roman Calendar. Orthodox: not a saint; the Russian Orthodox Encyclopedia calls him 'a saint of the Catholic Church'. Anglican, Episcopal and Lutheran calendars do not keep him.
status.source: Acta Sanctae Sedis 16 (1883), pp. 302-303 (decree of the Congregation of Rites, 15 December 1883, ratified by Leo XIII the same day); Catholic Encyclopedia; Roman Martyrology (via Cathopedia); USCCB, 23 October 2026 (Optional Memorial of Saint John of Capistrano); Orthodox Encyclopedia ('св. католич. Церкви (пам. 23 окт.)'); Church of England, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, LCMS, ELW (no entry)

patron_of.text: No patronage found in any source checked. Leave the line out.
patron_of.source: Catholic Encyclopedia, Acta Sanctae Sedis decree, Vatican News, santodelgiorno.it, Cathopedia, Orthodox Encyclopedia: none names a patronage.
patron_of.note: Wikidata lists no patronage either (research/people-audit.json: patronOfItems 0). Do not print one.

in_art.text: A scholar in a cap, often in prison or in bed, with Lady Philosophy beside him: a tall crowned woman with books and a staff. The wheel of Fortune often turns nearby.
in_art.source: Consolation, Book 1, prose 1 (Philosophy's look: 'Her right hand held a note-book; in her left she bore a staff'); Getty Museum MS 42 leaves, Coëtivy Master, about 1460-1470 (Philosophy with Boethius; Fortune turning the wheel); Utrecht University Library Hs. 1335 (Wheel of Fortune; Boethius on his sickbed); BnF Néerlandais 1 (about 1492); Mattia Preti, Boethius and Philosophy (about 1680); Orthodox Encyclopedia (his image is in medieval miniatures and on the portal of Chartres Cathedral)
in_art.note: A description of the pictures that survive, checked by looking at them on Commons. No source names a fixed attribute for him.
in_art.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "crowned" removed. The Consolation (1.1) gives her a note-book and a staff; our own band picture shows her in a white headdress, not a crown. Page now says: "In his book she holds a notebook and a staff."

wrote.text: The Consolation of Philosophy, in 5 books. Five short theological treatises, one of them doubted. Latin translations of Aristotle's logic and of Porphyry, with commentaries. Textbooks on arithmetic and music.
wrote.source: Stewart and Rand, Introduction ('He translated the Εἰσαγωγή of Porphyry, and the whole of Aristotle's Organon ... He adapted the arithmetic of Nicomachus, and his textbook on music ... His five theological Tractates'); Catholic Encyclopedia (De fide catholica 'generally regarded as spurious'); Loeb note to Tractate IV (now thought genuine); SEP section 1
wrote.note: Do not print a total count of works: the sources count differently (lost works, doubtful ones). The music textbook: Stewart and Rand say it 'was in use at Oxford and Cambridge until modern times'.
wrote.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "five short works on the Trinity and on Christ" was wrong: Tractate 3 (How substances can be good) and Tractate 4 (On the Catholic faith) are neither. Page now says "five short works of theology".

pronounced.source: Merriam-Webster, 'Boethius' (biographical name): 'Bo·​e·​thi·​us bō-ˈē-thē-əs'; Dictionary.com: '[boh-ee-thee-uhs]', stress on the second syllable ('boʊˈi θi əs'); Collins (via The Free Dictionary): '(bəʊˈiːθɪəs)'
pronounced.note: Merriam-Webster and Collins blocked plain fetches; Merriam-Webster was read with a browser user-agent (dict-mw-boethius.txt). Collins's form was read through The Free Dictionary's copy.

roles.name: Scholar
roles.text: His plan was to translate and explain all of Plato and Aristotle. He finished much of Aristotle's logic.
roles.source: Stewart and Rand, Introduction ('nothing less than the transmission to his countrymen of all the works of Plato and Aristotle'); SEP section 2 (the plan, announced in his second commentary on On Interpretation, c. 516)

roles.name: Consul
roles.text: He held the consulship alone in 510.
roles.source: James, Proem ('He was sole Consul in 510 A.D.'); Stewart and Rand ('consul under Theodoric the Ostrogoth in 510'); Hodgkin ('the Fasti Consulares')

roles.name: Master of Offices
roles.text: Theodoric made him Master of Offices, 'head of the whole civil administration', in 522.
roles.source: James, Proem ('raised by Theodoric to the dignity of Magister Officiorum, or head of the whole civil administration'); Hodgkin ('investiture with the office of Magister Officiorum on September 1, 522'); Anonymus Valesianus 85 (Rolfe renders magister officiorum 'master of ceremonies')

roles.name: Prisoner
roles.line: Wrote the Consolation in his cell
roles.text: Condemned unheard, he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy while he waited to die.
roles.source: Stewart and Rand ('He was thrown into prison at Pavia, where he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy'); Catholic Encyclopedia; Consolation 1.4 ('unheard and undefended')

summary.text: One feast, and only in the Catholic Church: 23 October, kept at Pavia and printed in the Roman Martyrology. No Orthodox, Anglican, Episcopal or Lutheran calendar keeps him.
summary.note: Print the West column with one entry and the East column as 'Not kept'. The General Roman Calendar has St John of Capistrano on 23 October.

catholic.text: 23 October. The Diocese of Pavia keeps it (a solemnity at his church there). The Roman Martyrology lists him that day: 'At Pavia, commemoration of Saint Severinus Boethius, martyr, who, famous for his learning and his writings, while shut in prison wrote a treatise on the consolation of philosophy, and served God with integrity until the death inflicted on him by King Theodoric.'
catholic.italian: A Pavia, commemorazione di san Severino Boezio, martire, che, illustre per la sua cultura e i suoi scritti, mentre era rinchiuso in carcere scrisse un trattato sulla consolazione della filosofia e servì con integrità Dio fino alla morte inflittagli dal re Teodorico.
catholic.source: Roman Martyrology (current Latin edition, in the Italian of the Italian bishops), 23 October, no. 6, as quoted by Cathopedia and by santodelgiorno.it; Basilica di San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro ('Oggi, 23 Ottobre, cade la solennità di San Severino Boezio'); Acta Sanctae Sedis 16 (1883); Catholic Encyclopedia ('honouring St. Severinus Boethius, on the 23rd of October'); USCCB readings for 23 October 2026 (Optional Memorial of Saint John of Capistrano: he is not in the General Roman Calendar)
catholic.note: The English is my plain rendering of the Italian, for our voice only; do not print it as a quotation. The Vatican's Latin Martyrologium Romanum (2004) was not fetched: the entry is read in the Italian quoted by two Catholic sites. The Catholic Encyclopedia says the 23 October feast was kept 'in many places' by the eighth century. The 1916 English Roman Martyrology was not checked for him (it is a different, older edition).
catholic.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the 1916 English Roman Martyrology (archive.org romanmartyrology00cathuoft, 23 October, pp. 326-328) was checked: it has NO entry for Boethius anywhere (23 October lists Servandus and Germanus, Theodore of Antioch, Peter Paschasius, Ignatius of Constantinople, Severin of Cologne, Romanus, Verus, Domitius, Benedict, John of Capistran). He is in today's Martyrology only. Page now says so.

orthodox.text: Not kept. He has no feast in the Orthodox calendars. The Russian Orthodox Encyclopedia describes him as 'a saint of the Catholic Church (commemorated 23 October)'.
orthodox.source: Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya, edited under Patriarch Kirill), 'Boethius'; OCA lives of saints for 23 October 2026 (Macarius the Roman, James the Brother of the Lord, Ignatius of Constantinople, Elisha of Lavreshev and others: no Boethius)
orthodox.note: The OCA site search for 'Boethius' returned a page with no results listed (it may load results by script, so it proves little). No Orthodox body or calendar was found that keeps him.

anglican.text: Not kept. The Church of England's Common Worship calendar has no Boethius.
anglican.source: Church of England, 'The Calendar' (Common Worship): no match for Boethius/Boetius/Severinus; its October list runs Remigius, Shaftesbury ... and has no 23 October commemoration of him

episcopal.text: Not kept. He is not in Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022.
episcopal.source: The Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (PDF, full text search: no Boethius/Boetius/Severinus)

lutheran.text: Not kept. Neither the LCMS commemorations nor the ELCA's Evangelical Lutheran Worship calendar lists him.
lutheran.source: LCMS, 'Commemorations' (lcms.org); Evangelical Lutheran Worship, the church year (Renewing Worship PDF, 2006, archived)

why.text: No source explains why 23 October. No ancient source records the day of his death.
why.source: Anonymus Valesianus 87 gives no date; Catholic Encyclopedia gives only the feast day.
why.note: Do not print 'the day he died' as a fact.

lines: He gave the speech for the king
numbers.text: In 522 both his young sons were consuls together. He gave the speech praising the king in the senate.
numbers.exact: That day when thou didst see thy two sons ride forth from home joint consuls, followed by a train of senators, and welcomed by the good-will of the people
numbers.source: Consolation, Book 2, prose 3 (Philosophy speaking); Cassiodorus, Anecdoton Holderi (Latin in Hodgkin: 'Qui regem Theodorichum in Senatu pro Consulatu filiorum luculenta oratione laudavit'); James, Proem
numbers.note: Philosophy adds that Fortune gave him 'a boon which she had never before granted to any private person'.

lines: Rome to Pavia is 455 Roman miles
numbers.text: He was condemned 'unheard and undefended, at a distance of near five hundred miles away'.
numbers.exact: Now for my too great zeal towards the senate I have been condemned to outlawry and death, unheard and undefended, at a distance of near five hundred miles away.
numbers.source: Consolation, Book 1, prose 4 (the prisoner speaking); James's footnote C ('The distance from Rome to Pavia, the place of Boethius' imprisonment, is 455 Roman miles')
numbers.note: The Latin is 'quingentis fere passuum milibus procul' (about five hundred thousand paces). Anonymus Valesianus 87 agrees he was sentenced 'without giving him a hearing'.

numbers.text: The Consolation alternates prose and verse: 39 poems and 39 prose sections in 5 books.
numbers.src: Counted in H. R. James's translation
numbers.source: Count of James's headings (raw-gutenberg-14328-james.txt): Book 1, 7 poems and 6 prose; Book 2, 8 and 8; Book 3, 12 and 12; Book 4, 7 and 7; Book 5, 5 and 6. Split into 78 files by script.
numbers.note: James, Preface: 'its alternate prose and verse, skilfully fitted together like dialogue and chorus in a Greek play'. The Loeb Latin has the same 39 metres.

numbers.chip: Greek masters he put into Latin
numbers.text: Theodoric's letter says he translated Pythagoras, Ptolemy, Nicomachus, Euclid, Plato, Aristotle and Archimedes.
numbers.exact: You have translated Pythagoras the musician, Ptolemy the astronomer, Nicomachus the arithmetician, Euclid the geometer, Plato the theologian, Aristotle the logician, and have given back the mechanician Archimedes to his own Sicilian countrymen (who now speak Latin).
numbers.source: Cassiodorus, Variae 1.45, King Theodoric to Boetius (tr. Thomas Hodgkin, The Letters of Cassiodorus, 1886)
numbers.note: Pythagoras here means Pythagorean music theory. The Orthodox Encyclopedia says his Ptolemy, Archimedes and Euclid translations are lost; what survives is the Aristotle, Porphyry, arithmetic (after Nicomachus) and music. Hodgkin's version of the Variae is partly condensed, but this passage is printed as translation, in quotation marks.
numbers.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the seven names are the king's letter's list (Variae 1.45), not an audited count. Page lines now: "Named in a letter from the king", "Several of these are lost" (Orthodox Encyclopedia: Ptolemy and Archimedes not preserved).

numbers.text: If he was born about 480 and killed in 524, he was about 44. On other dates, up to about 50.
numbers.src: Catholic Encyclopedia; Stewart and Rand; SEP
numbers.source: Born about 480 (Catholic Encyclopedia, Stewart and Rand, Orthodox Encyclopedia); died 524 (Stewart and Rand; Catholic Encyclopedia '524 or 525'), or 526 (SEP; Orthodox Encyclopedia gives both). SEP puts the birth at 475-7.
numbers.note: A computed number: print it as 'about', with the two dates in the lines. Drop it if the page wants only numbers a source states outright.

lines: On the Trinity, and on Christ
numbers.text: Five short treatises on the Trinity and on Christ. Cassiodorus names his book on the Trinity and his book against Nestorius. The fourth, On the Catholic Faith, lacks his name in the best manuscripts.
numbers.exact: His five theological Tractates are here, together with the Consolation of Philosophy, to speak for themselves.
numbers.source: Stewart and Rand, Introduction and note 43; Hodgkin (Anecdoton Holderi); Catholic Encyclopedia ('De Fide Catholica (generally regarded as spurious...)')
numbers.note: Stewart and Rand, note 43: the fourth tractate, 'though lacking, in the best MSS., either an ascription to Boethius or a title, is firmly imbedded in two distinct recensions ... There is no reason to disturb it.'

traits.title: stood by the accused
traits.text: When a senator, Albinus, was accused of treason, Boethius spoke up before the king. He said, 'The charge of Cyprianus is false, but if Albinus did that, so also have I and the whole senate with one accord done it; it is false, my Lord King.' The accuser then produced false witnesses against Boethius too.
traits.exact: The charge of Cyprianus is false, but if Albinus did that, so also have I and the whole senate with one accord done it; it is false, my Lord King.
traits.latin: Falsa est insinuatio Cypriani; sed si Albinus fecit, et ego et cunctus senatus uno consilio fecimus; falsum est, domne rex.
traits.note: Tr. J. C. Rolfe (Loeb 1939). Thayer's LacusCurtius marks this page public domain (one asterisk in the URL: 'A page or image on this site is in the public domain ONLY if its URL has a total of one * asterisk'). The Anonymus is a chronicle written soon after Theodoric's reign; it is hostile to the king.

traits.title: no friend to the powerful
traits.text: He says he took office to put philosophy into practice. He fought the king's officials when they preyed on the weak, and he stopped a forced grain sale that would have starved Campania.
traits.exact: I have had to think nothing of giving offence to the powerful in the cause of justice. How often have I encountered and balked Conigastus in his assaults on the fortunes of the weak?
traits.note: His own account, spoken as the prisoner. Procopius, writing soon after, says he and Symmachus were 'mindful of justice in a manner surpassed by no other men' (Wars 5.1.33).
traits.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "grain" is not in James (1.4 says "a forced sale ... at a season of grievous scarcity"). Page now: "a forced sale in a time of famine".

traits.title: honest about what he did not know
traits.text: At a church meeting in Rome, everyone loudly claimed a hard question about Christ was obvious. He kept quiet, went home and thought it through, and then wrote his treatise Against Eutyches and Nestorius.
traits.exact: I was, I admit, much put out, and being overwhelmed by the mob of ignorant speakers, I held my peace, fearing lest I should be rightly set down as insane if I held out for being sane among those madmen.
traits.exact2: my possible contribution was less by one thing, namely, the false assumption of a knowledge that I had not got
traits.note: Tr. Stewart and Rand (1918). Their note dates the Eastern bishops' letter behind the meeting to 512; SEP says c. 513. He then 'continued to ponder all the questions in my mind, not swallowing what I had heard, but rather chewing the cud of constant meditation'.
traits.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the preface does not say "in Rome", "church meeting" or "went home". Page now: "At a meeting, a letter from Eastern bishops to the Pope was read out" (Loeb note 43: the letter to Pope Symmachus) and "held his peace and thought it through".

traits.title: wrote for the few
traits.text: He wrote his treatise on the Trinity in hard, new words on purpose, for his father-in-law alone. He said so plainly.
traits.exact: So I purposely use brevity and wrap up the ideas I draw from the deep questionings of philosophy in new and unaccustomed words which speak only to you and to myself, that is, if you deign to look at them. The rest of the world I simply disregard: they cannot understand, and therefore do not deserve to read.
traits.note: Tr. Stewart and Rand. The same preface: 'You must however examine whether the seeds sown in my mind by St. Augustine's writings have borne fruit.'

traits.title: a maker of clocks, a judge of music
traits.text: King Theodoric asked him to have a water-clock and a sundial made as a gift for the king of the Burgundians. He also asked him to choose a first-rate harper for Clovis, king of the Franks.
traits.exact: Exert yourself therefore, oh Boetius, to get this thing put in hand.
traits.exact2: We felt that in you lay our best chance of complying with his request, because you, being such a lover of music yourself, will be able to introduce us to the right man.
traits.cite: Cassiodorus, Variae, Book 1, letter 45, and Book 2, letter 40
traits.note: Tr. Hodgkin, 1886. Another letter (Variae 1.10) asks him to look into short-weight coins paid to the guards.

traits.title: low, then lifted
traits.text: The book opens with him in tears, writing sad verses with the Muses at his bed. Philosophy drives them out and spends five books talking him back to sense. He wrote himself as the patient.
traits.exact: Who,' said she, 'has allowed yon play-acting wantons to approach this sick man--these who, so far from giving medicine to heal his malady, even feed it with sweet poison?
traits.note: The opening poem, in the prisoner's voice: 'Now perforce in tears and sadness / Learn a mournful strain to raise.' Philosophy's words about the Muses; the 'sick man' is Boethius.

others_on_him.who: Procopius of Caesarea, historian, writing about 25 years after his death
others_on_him.exact: But because they practised philosophy and were mindful of justice in a manner surpassed by no other men, relieving the destitution of both citizens and strangers by generous gifts of money, they attained great fame and thus led men of the basest sort to envy them.
others_on_him.cite: History of the Wars, Book 5, chapter 1
others_on_him.note: Of Symmachus and 'his son-in-law Boetius'. Tr. H. B. Dewing (Loeb 1919), LacusCurtius, marked public domain. 'Writing about 25 years after': Procopius wrote the Gothic War in the 550s; that date is general knowledge, not from this page. Safer wording: 'Procopius, a historian of the next generation'.

others_on_him.who: King Theodoric, in a letter drafted by Cassiodorus (the king who later had him killed)
others_on_him.exact: You have thoroughly imbued yourself with Greek philosophy.
others_on_him.note: Tr. Hodgkin. Hodgkin's footnote: the Latin 'sic enim Atheniensium scholas longe positus introisti' does not mean he went to Athens.

others_on_him.who: Cassiodorus, his colleague and kinsman, in a note on his family
others_on_him.exact: He wrote a book concerning the Holy Trinity, and certain dogmatic chapters, and a book against Nestorius.
others_on_him.latin: Scripsit librum de Sancta Trinitate et capita quaedam dogmatica et librum contra Nestorium.
others_on_him.note: The fragment was found by Alfred Holder and published by Usener in 1877. It is the proof that the Christian treatises are his (Catholic Encyclopedia; Stewart and Rand). Hodgkin: Symmachus and Boethius 'were relations of Cassiodorus'. The same fragment: 'Utraque lingua peritissimus orator fuit' (he was a most skilled orator in both languages, Latin and Greek).

others_on_him.who: Dante, about 800 years later, placing him among the wise in heaven
others_on_him.exact: The sainted soul, which the fallacious world Makes manifest to him who listeneth well
others_on_him.note: Tr. Longfellow (1867). Dante does not name him; he is the eighth light, whose body lies 'in Cieldauro'. Vatican News: Dante 'lo chiamava "anima santa"'.

others_on_him.exact: The senator Boethius is the last of the Romans whom Cato or Tully could have acknowledged for their countryman.
others_on_him.cite: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, chapter 39
others_on_him.note: Gibbon calls the Consolation 'a golden volume not unworthy of the leisure of Plato or Tully'. Chapter 39 is in Gutenberg's Volume 4 (eBook 893); the 1781 date of that volume of the first edition is general knowledge.

life_moments.title: An orphan in a great house
life_moments.text: His father, a former consul, died when he was small. He grew up in the house of Symmachus, a senator admired for his character and learning. Later he married Symmachus's daughter, Rusticiana.
life_moments.exact: I say nothing of how, when orphaned and desolate, thou wast taken into the care of illustrious men; how thou wast chosen for alliance with the highest in the state

life_moments.title: Greek into Latin
life_moments.text: He set out to put all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin, with notes. He finished much of Aristotle's logic, and wrote textbooks on arithmetic and music. For centuries the West read Aristotle through him.
life_moments.cite: Stewart and Rand, Introduction; SEP section 2; Catholic Encyclopedia
life_moments.note: Catholic Encyclopedia: 'the schoolmen, down to the beginning of the twelfth century, depended entirely on Boethius for their knowledge of Aristotle's doctrines.' SEP: his social position 'ensured that he was taught Greek thoroughly'.

life_moments.title: Clocks for a king
life_moments.text: King Theodoric used his learning in diplomacy. He had Boethius arrange a water-clock and a sundial for the king of the Burgundians, and pick a harper for Clovis, king of the Franks.
life_moments.cite: Cassiodorus, Variae, Book 1, letter 45; Book 2, letter 40
life_moments.note: Hodgkin dates the Clovis letter to about 503 or 504, when Boethius was in his twenties.
life_moments.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: no source places the clock letter; page place is now "Italy".

life_moments.title: Consul
life_moments.text: He was consul alone in 510. 'The highest honours of the State came to him unsought,' writes his translator James.
life_moments.cite: James, Proem; Stewart and Rand, Introduction
life_moments.note: James's Proem is a modern (1897) summary, not an ancient source.

life_moments.title: Silent in the meeting
life_moments.text: A letter from Eastern bishops about Christ's two natures was read out. Everyone shouted that the answer was obvious. He said nothing, went home, worked it out, and wrote Against Eutyches and Nestorius for his friend John the deacon.
life_moments.cite: Against Eutyches and Nestorius, preface; Stewart and Rand, note 43 (date 512)

life_moments.title: The best day of his life
life_moments.text: His two young sons were made consuls together. They rode to the senate house with the senators behind them. He gave the speech praising the king, then sat between his sons at the Circus and handed out gifts to the crowd. That year the king made him Master of Offices.
life_moments.exact: when in the Circus, seated between the two consuls, thou didst glut the multitude thronging around with the triumphal largesses for which they looked
life_moments.cite: Consolation, Book 2, prose 3; James, Proem; Hodgkin

life_moments.title: "Then I did it too"
life_moments.text: An informer, Cyprian, accused the senator Albinus of writing treason to the emperor at Constantinople. Before the king, Boethius said that if Albinus was guilty, so was he and the whole senate. Cyprian found false witnesses against him too. The king believed them.
life_moments.cite: Anonymus Valesianus, part 2, sections 85 and 86; Consolation, Book 1, prose 4 (Verona)
life_moments.note: The Consolation places the king's attack on the senate over Albinus 'at Verona'. The year 523: Orthodox Encyclopedia; Hodgkin puts the charge 'before the end of' 522.

life_moments.title: Condemned unheard
life_moments.text: He was held first in a church's baptistery, then on an estate near Pavia. The senate itself condemned him, far away in Rome, without a hearing. The charges were treason, and sacrilege: using dark arts to get ahead. In his cell he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy.
life_moments.exact: they falsely asserted that in the pursuit of my ambition I had stained my conscience with sacrilegious acts
life_moments.note: Consolation 1.4: 'Of a truth the senate, by its decrees concerning me, has made it such!' The Catholic Encyclopedia glosses 'sacrilege' as 'the practice of astrology'; SEP says 'engaging in magic'. Latin places of custody: 'ad baptisterium ecclesiae' and 'in agro Calventiano, ubi in custodia habebatur'.

life_moments.title: Killed
life_moments.text: The king sent men to kill him where he was held. They twisted a cord round his head for a long time, then beat him to death with a club.

of_him.text: None. No early source tells of a miracle worked by him or at his tomb. Leave the miracles section out.
of_him.source: Anonymus Valesianus (the only near-contemporary account of his death) records none for him; it does record a healing at the funeral of Pope John I (section 93), which is not his. The 1883 decree gives no miracles; it confirms an immemorial cult.
of_him.note: Procopius's story of Theodoric seeing Symmachus's face in a fish head (Wars 5.1.35-39) is a portent told of the king, not a miracle of Boethius. It belongs in 'How he died' (the aftermath), told as Procopius tells it.

framing.text: Most lines come from the Consolation, a dialogue he wrote in prison. The prisoner, 'Boethius', complains; Lady Philosophy answers. Each line says who speaks. The treatise lines are in his own voice.

feature.exact: For truly in adverse fortune the worst sting of misery is to have been happy.
feature.kicker: Remembering his sons' great day, in prison
feature.latin: Nam in omni aduersitate fortunae infelicissimum est genus infortunii fuisse felicem.
feature.speaker: The prisoner (Boethius himself)
feature.ctx: Dante gave the thought to Francesca in the Inferno: 'There is no greater sorrow / Than to be mindful of the happy time / In misery' (Longfellow).
feature.note: James italicises 'have been'. The Latin is the Loeb text (it prints 'aduersitate' for 'adversitate'). The Catholic Encyclopedia links Dante and Tennyson's 'a sorrow's crown of sorrow' to this line.

lines.exact: So true is it that nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so, and conversely every lot is happy if borne with equanimity.
lines.speaker: Philosophy
lines.ctx: On his exile: 'This very place which thou callest exile is to them that dwell therein their native land' comes just before.
lines.latin: adeo nihil est miserum nisi cum putes contraque beata sors omnis est aequanimitate tolerantis.
lines.note: James borrows Hamlet's words ('there is nothing either good or bad but thinking makes it so', Act 2, scene 2). The Latin is plainer: 'nothing is wretched unless you think it so'. See misquoted.

lines.exact: For truly I believe that Ill Fortune is of more use to men than Good Fortune.
lines.speaker: Philosophy
lines.ctx: Good Fortune always lies, she says; Ill Fortune tells the truth. 'The one deceives, the other teaches.'
lines.exact_more: The one deceives, the other teaches

lines.exact: Cease, then, to seek the wealth thou hast lost, since in true friends thou hast found the most precious of all riches.
lines.speaker: Philosophy
lines.ctx: His fall showed him who his real friends were.

lines.exact: I turn the wheel that spins. I delight to see the high come down and the low ascend.
lines.speaker: Fortune, as Philosophy makes her speak
lines.ctx: The source of the medieval 'wheel of Fortune' pictures.
lines.note: Philosophy speaks in Fortune's voice through this prose section.

lines.exact: What law can lovers move? A higher law is love!
lines.speaker: Philosophy, in a poem about Orpheus
lines.ctx: Orpheus turned back for Eurydice at the gates of hell, and lost her.
lines.latin: Quis legem det amantibus? Maior lex amor est sibi.

lines.exact: Now, eternity is the possession of endless life whole and perfect at a single moment.
lines.speaker: Philosophy
lines.ctx: His answer to how God can know what we will choose without forcing us: God sees all time at once.
lines.latin: Aeternitas igitur est interminabilis uitae tota simul et perfecta possessio
lines.note: SEP: this definition 'became the starting-point for almost every later medieval discussion of God and time'.

lines.exact: The individual substance of a rational nature.
lines.translation: H. F. Stewart and E. K. Rand, Loeb Classical Library, 1918
lines.speaker: Boethius (his own voice)
lines.ctx: His definition of a person. The Middle Ages used it for centuries.
lines.note: Catholic Encyclopedia: the schoolmen 'adopted his definitions ... for instance, the definitions of "person", "eternity"'.

lines.exact: If God exists, whence comes evil? Yet whence comes good, if He exists not?
lines.speaker: The prisoner, quoting "one of thy disciples"
lines.ctx: In his cell, asking why God lets the wicked win.
lines.note: He is quoting an unnamed philosopher, not stating his own view.

lines.exact: Great is the necessity of righteousness laid upon you if ye will not hide it from yourselves, seeing that all your actions are done before the eyes of a Judge who seeth all things.
lines.display: Great is the necessity of righteousness laid upon you if ye will not hide it from yourselves, seeing that all your actions are done before the eyes of a Judge Who seeth all things.
lines.speaker: Philosophy: the last words of the book

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'There is no greater sorrow than to remember happy times in misery.' (Dante)
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Dante wrote it, but the thought is Boethius's first. In prison he wrote that 'the worst sting of misery is to have been happy'.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: There is no greater sorrow Than to be mindful of the happy time In misery
misquoted_or_legend.cite: Dante, Inferno, Canto 5 (Longfellow); Consolation, Book 2, prose 4; Catholic Encyclopedia
misquoted_or_legend.note: The Catholic Encyclopedia: the lines Tennyson paraphrases 'are themselves at least a haunting memory of Boethius'. Francesca adds 'and that thy Teacher knows': some read the Teacher as Boethius, others as Virgil. Do not print either reading as fact.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'Nothing is good or bad but thinking makes it so' is a line of Boethius.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: That is Hamlet. James's 1897 translation borrowed Hamlet's words for Boethius's plainer Latin, 'nihil est miserum nisi cum putes' (nothing is wretched unless you think it so).
misquoted_or_legend.exact: there is nothing either good or bad but thinking makes it so
misquoted_or_legend.cite: Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 2, scene 2; Consolation, Book 2, prose 4 (Latin, Loeb)
misquoted_or_legend.note: Act and scene are the standard numbering; the Gutenberg file's own headings were not checked for them.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'If you had kept silent, you would have stayed a philosopher' (Si tacuisses, philosophus mansisses).
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Not his sentence. He tells a story of a man who boasted he was a philosopher because he bore insults patiently. The reply was, 'I should have hadst thou held thy peace.' The Latin proverb is a later retelling.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: The other, with biting sarcasm, retorted: "I should have hadst thou held thy peace."
misquoted_or_legend.note: 'A later retelling' is our wording; no source fetched dates the proverb. Safer: 'The proverb is not in his book.'
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the Latin of 2.7 (Gutenberg 13316) DOES have "si tacuisses" ("Intellexeram, inquit, si tacuisses"); only "philosophus mansisses" is missing. Also the man did not boast "because he bore insults": he was challenged to bear them, bore them, then boasted. Page rewritten to say "Only the first half".

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He was martyred by an Arian king for the Catholic faith.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The earliest sources say he was condemned for treason and sacrilege, after defending a senator. Pavia honoured him as a martyr from early on, and Rome confirmed that cult in 1883. The Catholic Encyclopedia admits 'it is not easy to show from documentary sources that he died a martyr for the Catholic Faith'.
misquoted_or_legend.cite: Anonymus Valesianus 85-87; Consolation, Book 1, prose 4; Catholic Encyclopedia; Acta Sanctae Sedis 16 (1883)
misquoted_or_legend.note: Both sides go in 'Is he a saint?'. santodelgiorno.it (Catholic): 'la sua esecuzione ebbe motivazioni politiche' (his execution had political motives). The 1883 decree says Theodoric set out to destroy three Catholic leaders, Pope John, Symmachus and Boethius.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He wrote the Consolation in the tower of Pavia, and was beheaded with a sword.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Later tradition. The earliest account says he was held in a baptistery, then on the Calventian estate, and killed with a cord and a club. The sword and the tower come from later tellings, which the 1883 decree repeats.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: he composed, in the tower of Pavia, the Consolation of Philosophy
misquoted_or_legend.cite: Anonymus Valesianus 87; Acta Sanctae Sedis 16 (1883), p. 303 ("Ticinum deportatus ac in turri occlusus, gladio percussus occubuit"); Gibbon, chapter 39 ("in the tower of Pavia"); James, Epilogue
misquoted_or_legend.note: James's Epilogue gives both versions: 'According to one account, he was cut down by the swords of the soldiers before the very judgment-seat of Theodoric; according to another, a cord was first fastened round his forehead'. Commons files him under 'decapitation'.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: The Consolation never mentions Christ, so he was not really a Christian, or gave up the faith in prison.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: His treatises on the Trinity and on Christ are his: Cassiodorus, who knew him, names them. The Consolation is written as philosophy, by reason alone. Scholars have argued over the silence for centuries, but that he was a Christian is not in doubt.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: Boethius was without doubt a Christian, a Doctor and perhaps a martyr.
misquoted_or_legend.cite: Stewart and Rand, Introduction (1918); Cassiodorus, Anecdoton Holderi; Catholic Encyclopedia
misquoted_or_legend.note: Hodgkin (1886), writing before the fragment was widely known in England, shows how strong the doubt had been: 'the name of Christ is never once mentioned'.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He invented the wheel of Fortune.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: No. Cicero already speaks of 'the wheel of Fortune' (fortunae rotam) in a speech five centuries earlier. Boethius made the image famous: his Fortune says, 'I turn the wheel that spins.'
misquoted_or_legend.exact: ne tum quidem fortunae rotam pertimescebat
misquoted_or_legend.cite: Cicero, Against Piso (Latin, The Latin Library); Consolation, Book 2, prose 2
misquoted_or_legend.note: 'Made the image famous' is our judgement from the many medieval pictures; no source fetched says it in so many words. The section number of the Cicero passage (usually cited as In Pisonem 22) was not confirmed in the fetched file.
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: In Pisonem (55 BC; Cicero died 43 BC) is nearly six centuries before the Consolation (c. 524), not five. Page says "nearly six centuries earlier".

misquoted_or_legend.truth: Gibbon's words, with a qualifier: 'the last of the Romans whom Cato or Tully could have acknowledged for their countryman'. Stewart and Rand called him 'the last of the Roman philosophers, and the first of the scholastic theologians'.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: Boethius was the last of the Roman philosophers, and the first of the scholastic theologians.
misquoted_or_legend.cite: Gibbon, chapter 39; Stewart and Rand, Introduction

hard_topics.holder: The 1883 decree (Latin) tells it as a martyrdom: Theodoric, 'a most bitter follower of the Arian heresy', resolved to destroy three Catholic leaders, Pope John, Symmachus and Boethius. It adds that the king had the body buried in secret, fearing Catholics would honour him as a martyr. The Roman Martyrology calls him 'martire'.
hard_topics.holder_exact: acerrimus , uti erat, Arianae haeresis sectator
hard_topics.critics: The Anonymus Valesianus says the charge was treason, over letters to the emperor Justin, and the Consolation says treason and sacrilege. The Catholic Encyclopedia: 'it is not easy to show from documentary sources that he died a martyr for the Catholic Faith.' santodelgiorno.it: his execution 'had political motives'. Stewart and Rand: 'perhaps a martyr'.
hard_topics.critics_exact: though it is not easy to show from documentary sources that he died a martyr for the Catholic Faith
hard_topics.source: Acta Sanctae Sedis 16 (1883), pp. 302-303; Anonymus Valesianus 85-87; Consolation 1.4; Catholic Encyclopedia
hard_topics.note: Context both sides accept: Theodoric was an Arian Christian, the emperor Justin was acting against Arians in the East, and Pope John I died in Theodoric's prison soon after (Anonymus Valesianus 88-93). The decree's 'acerrimus , uti erat' keeps the OCR's stray space.

hard_topics.topic: Why does the Consolation never name Christ?
hard_topics.holder: Stewart and Rand: 'In the Consolation he is writing philosophy; in the Tractates he is writing theology.' The Catholic Encyclopedia notes hints that 'there are more potent remedies (validiora remedia)' beyond philosophy.
hard_topics.critics: Nineteenth-century critics said he was 'a pagan, or at best a luke-warm Christian, who at the end cast off the faith' (as Stewart and Rand sum them up). Hodgkin: 'the name of Christ is never once mentioned, the tone, though religious and reverential, is that of a Theist only'.
hard_topics.critics_exact: the name of Christ is never once mentioned
hard_topics.source: Stewart and Rand, Introduction; Catholic Encyclopedia; Hodgkin, Letters of Cassiodorus, introduction

hard_topics.topic: Plato's ideas in a Christian's book
hard_topics.holder: Philosophy teaches some things from Plato that Christians do not hold as doctrine: that all learning is remembering what the soul knew before ('We learn but that we have forgot'), a world-soul, and that the happy become 'gods' by sharing in God's nature, though 'in nature God is One only'.
hard_topics.exact: So every man who is happy is a god; and though in nature God is One only, yet there is nothing to hinder that very many should be gods by participation in that nature.
hard_topics.critics: The Catholic Encyclopedia: 'There are evident traces of the influence of the Neo-Platonists, especially of Proclus, and little, if anything, that can be said to reflect Christian influences.' Stewart and Rand answer that the argument 'is anything but Neoplatonic; it is all his own'.
hard_topics.critics_exact: There are evident traces of the influence of the Neo-Platonists
hard_topics.source: Consolation 3.10 and 3.11 (poem 'Reminiscence', with James's note on Plato's Meno and Phaedo), 3.9 (James: 'The substance of this poem is taken from Plato's Timaeus'); Catholic Encyclopedia; Stewart and Rand
hard_topics.note: The 'reminiscence' poem hedges: 'If Plato's teaching erreth not'.

hard_topics.holder: He wrote theology in hard words on purpose, for one reader: 'The rest of the world I simply disregard: they cannot understand, and therefore do not deserve to read.'
hard_topics.critics: No early critic found. Say it plainly and let it stand; it contrasts with preachers like Chrysostom and Augustine, who wrote for crowds (our observation, not a source's).
hard_topics.note: If the page prints the contrast with Chrysostom and Augustine, mark it as our reading or drop it.

where_he_stood.text: Seven of the quiz's 23 statements. Five show a line; two are on record but not quoted (quiet, surplus). Values from site/src/data/which-early-christian.json (people.boethius.cells). Three of the five lines are spoken by Philosophy in the Consolation, not by the prisoner: the book's settled view, but not his first-person voice. The two treatise lines are his own voice. Every line is word for word in the named translation.

rows.exact: Examine carefully what I have said, and if possible, reconcile faith and reason.
rows.cite: Whether Father, Son and Holy Spirit may be Substantially Predicated of the Divinity (Tractate 2), closing words
rows.translation: H. F. Stewart and E. K. Rand, Loeb Classical Library, 1918
rows.statement: Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith.
rows.place: Tractate 2, to John the Deacon, the last lines
rows.note: The full sentence: 'If I am right and speak in accordance with the Faith, I pray you confirm me. But if you are in any point of another opinion, examine carefully what I have said, and if possible, reconcile faith and reason.' The site's line starts mid-sentence with a capital E. Latin: 'fidem si poterit rationemque coniunge'. Fit to the statement: the line is about joining faith and reason, which suits the 'learn from philosophy' side; his whole career of translating pagan Greek philosophy is the stronger evidence (Stewart and Rand; Variae 1.45).

rows.exact: Pity is rather due to the criminal, who ought to be brought to the judgment-seat by his accusers in a spirit not of anger, but of compassion and kindness
rows.statement: Anger at real wrongdoing can be a good thing.
rows.note: James prints 'whereas pity is rather due...' in the middle of a sentence, which runs on after 'kindness' with a comma ('as a sick man to the physician'); the site capitalises 'Pity' and ends with a full stop. Nearby: 'for the wise no place is left for hatred'.

rows.exact: Joy, hope and fear Suffer not near, Drive grief away: Shackled and blind And lost is the mind Where these have sway.
rows.statement: The best way to live is free of strong emotions, with only a steady peace inside.
rows.place: Book 1, poem 7 (Philosophy's song, the last of Book 1)
rows.note: Printed as verse in James: six short lines.

rows.exact: I have long pondered this problem with such mind as I have and all the light that God has lent me.
rows.cite: On the Trinity (Tractate 1), preface, to Symmachus
rows.translation: H. F. Stewart and E. K. Rand, Loeb Classical Library, 1918
rows.statement: Some questions about God are better left alone.
rows.place: On the Trinity, the first sentence
rows.note: The same preface adds a limit: 'We should not of course press our inquiry further than man's wit and reason are allowed to climb the height of heavenly knowledge.'

rows.exact: Therefore, withstand vice, practise virtue, lift up your souls to right hopes, offer humble prayers to Heaven.
rows.statement: Becoming a better person is mostly down to your own effort.
rows.place: Book 5, prose 6 (Philosophy, near the end of the book)
rows.note: The sentence before it: 'Our hopes and prayers also are not fixed on God in vain, and when they are rightly directed cannot fail of effect.' So the line is not pure self-help; +1 (not +2) fits.

hidden.text: Hidden on the site. Candidate passages: the philosopher who should have 'held thy peace' (Book 2, prose 7), and his own silence at the meeting (Against Eutyches, preface).
Hidden on the site. Candidate passage: 'then money is only precious when it is given away, and, by being transferred to others, ceases to be one's own' (Book 2, prose 5, Philosophy).
hidden.exact: money is only precious when it is given away, and, by being transferred to others, ceases to be one's own

friends_family_rivals.text: The senator who raised him and whose daughter he married. Theodoric had him brought to Ravenna and killed soon after Boethius, fearing his grief would turn to revolt.
friends_family_rivals.exact: There the king, fearing that through resentment at the death of his son-in-law,
friends_family_rivals.note: Philosophy in prison: Symmachus is 'a man whose splendid character does honour to the human race' and still 'safe and unharmed'. The son-in-law hyphen in Rolfe is a non-breaking hyphen (normalised).

friends_family_rivals.text: Symmachus's daughter. Years later, in Rome's famine, she begged for bread; the Goths wanted her dead for pulling down Theodoric's statues to avenge her father and husband, but King Totila protected her.
friends_family_rivals.exact: Rusticiana, the daughter of Symmachus, who had been wife of Boethius, a woman who was always lavishing her wealth upon the needy
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: Procopius 7.20.26-27 puts her begging after Totila TOOK Rome (546), when the Goths plundered the city; not "in Rome's famine". Page now: "when the Goths took Rome".

friends_family_rivals.text: Made consuls together in 522, while still young. Theodoric's daughter later gave back their fathers' estates to the children of Symmachus and Boethius.
friends_family_rivals.exact: she even restored to the children of Symmachus and Boetius their fathers' estates
friends_family_rivals.note: 'she' is Amalasuntha, Theodoric's daughter, regent for her son.

friends_family_rivals.text: The friend he wrote three of his treatises for, calling him 'my saintly master and reverend father'. The Catholic Encyclopedia says he later became Pope John I.
friends_family_rivals.note: Identity with Pope John I is the Catholic Encyclopedia's claim ('afterwards Pope John I'); not all scholars accept it. Print 'probably'. Pope John I died in Theodoric's prison at Ravenna soon after Boethius (Anonymus Valesianus 93).

friends_family_rivals.text: The senator accused of writing to the emperor against Theodoric. Boethius defended him and fell with him.
The court official who brought the charge against Albinus, then produced false witnesses against Boethius.
Men he names as his accusers: Basil was sacked from the king's household and in debt; the other two were under sentence of banishment for fraud that very day.
friends_family_rivals.exact: one of my accusers is Basil, who, after being dismissed from the king's household, was driven by his debts to lodge an information against my name
friends_family_rivals.note: 'For fraud' is loose: James says 'for many and various offences'. Print 'for various crimes'.
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: 1.4 says Opilio and Gaudentius were condemned "for many and various offences" (not fraud), and "that same day" is the day the king ordered them out of Ravenna. Page now says so; "sacked" became "dismissed" (James's word).

friends_family_rivals.text: The Ostrogothic king of Italy, an Arian Christian. He trusted Boethius for years, then had him condemned unheard and killed. Procopius says he wept over it before he died.
friends_family_rivals.exact: wept for the wrong he had done Symmachus and Boetius

friends_family_rivals.text: A fellow statesman and a relative. He drafted the king's letters to Boethius and wrote the note that proves the Christian treatises are his.
friends_family_rivals.note: Hodgkin: Symmachus and Boethius 'were relations of Cassiodorus'.
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "proves" overstates Stewart and Rand ("sufficient confirmation of the manuscript tradition"). Page now: "confirms". "A relative": Hodgkin, Letters of Cassiodorus, on the Anecdoton ("Symmachus and Boethius, though they were relations of Cassiodorus").

friends_family_rivals.text: He hoped his book on the Trinity showed 'the seeds sown in my mind by St. Augustine's writings'. They now lie in the same church at Pavia.
friends_family_rivals.cite: On the Trinity, preface; Orthodox Encyclopedia
friends_family_rivals.exact: You must however examine whether the seeds sown in my mind by St. Augustine's writings have borne fruit.
friends_family_rivals.note: On CCEL's page a footnote ('5 5 e.g. Aug. De Trin.') is printed inside the sentence; the Gutenberg Loeb text has it clean.

friends_family_rivals.text: The two heretics of opposite errors about Christ. He wrote to refute both and set out 'the middle way of the Christian Faith'.
friends_family_rivals.exact: I will temperately set forth the middle way of the Christian Faith

how_he_died.text: Killed near Pavia, in 524 or perhaps 526, on King Theodoric's orders, without a hearing. They tied a cord round his forehead and twisted it for a long time, then beat him to death with a club. No last words are recorded.
how_he_died.exact: He was tortured for a long time with a cord bound about his forehead so tightly that his eyes cracked in their sockets, and finally, while under torture, he was beaten to death with a cudgel.

aftermath.text: The king then had Symmachus brought to Ravenna and killed. Pope John I, sent to Constantinople and treated as an enemy on his return, died a few days later.

Procopius tells that a few days later a great fish's head was set before Theodoric at dinner. He saw in it the face of Symmachus, newly slain, and fled to his bed shivering. He told his doctor, wept for the wrong he had done Symmachus and Boetius, and died not long after.
aftermath.exact: This seemed to Theoderic to be the head of Symmachus newly slain.
aftermath.cite: Procopius, History of the Wars, Book 5, chapter 1
aftermath.note: Procopius calls it Theodoric's 'first and last act of injustice' to his subjects. Theodoric died in 526 (Anonymus Valesianus 95-96 gives the day of the week and month, not the year).

later.text: Later tellings say he was shut in a tower at Pavia and killed with the sword. The 1883 decree repeats this, and adds that Theodoric had him buried in secret.
later.cite: Acta Sanctae Sedis 16 (1883), p. 303; James, Epilogue
later.exact: the swords of the soldiers before the very judgment-seat of Theodoric

how_he_died.note: The Consolation itself ends before his death; no prayer or words at death are recorded by any source.
how_he_died.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: no fetched source says the Anonymus was "written soon after" Theodoric's reign or is the "earliest" account. Hodgkin (index) calls it "an unknown chronicler of the Sixth Century". Page now: "A short chronicle by an unknown writer of the sixth century ... It turns against the king in his last years." Symmachus: AV 92 says the king feared "resentment at the death of his son-in-law" might lead him "to take some step in opposition to his rule", and killed him "under a false accusation"; page no longer says "avenge". Procopius 5.1.37: Theodoric ran to his chamber and had covers heaped on him, not "fled to his bed".

is_he_a_saint.text: Yes, for Catholics, as a local saint. Pavia has honoured him as a martyr since the early Middle Ages, and Rome confirmed that cult in 1883. He is not in the Church's general calendar. The Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans do not count him a saint.

churches.note: Cult at Pavia confirmed 15 December 1883; in the Roman Martyrology on 23 October
'A saint of the Catholic Church' (Orthodox Encyclopedia)

Not in the LCMS or ELCA calendars

quotes.exact: The local cult of Boethius at Pavia was sanctioned when, in 1883, the Sacred Congregation of Rites confirmed the custom prevailing in that diocese of honouring St. Severinus Boethius, on the 23rd of October.
Boethius was without doubt a Christian, a Doctor and perhaps a martyr.

is_he_a_saint.note: Honest caveat for the page: he was condemned on political charges, and the martyr title rests on the Pavia tradition, which Rome confirmed as an immemorial cult (not a canonisation process). The Orthodox Encyclopedia uses the word 'canonised' ('официально канонизировала') for the 1883 act. Pope Benedict XVI visited his tomb on 22 April 2007 (the basilica's own page).

prayer_he_wrote.text: Two prayers to God stand in the Consolation, in verse. One is the prisoner's own (Book 1, poem 5, which James titles 'Boethius' Prayer'). The other Philosophy sings before she shows him the highest good (Book 3, poem 9). Both are his compositions. The second follows Plato's Timaeus closely (James's note).

items.exact: Sovereign Ruler, Lord of all! Can it be that Thou disdainest Only man?
items.speaker: The prisoner
items.exact_more: Sore we toss on fortune's tide; Master, bid the waves subside! And earth's ways with consummation Of Thy heaven's order guide!

items.exact: Oh, grant, almighty Father, Grant us on reason's wing to soar aloft To heaven's exalted height; grant us to see The fount of good; grant us, the true light found, To fix our steadfast eyes in vision clear On Thee.
items.speaker: Philosophy
items.exact_more: For Thou art The true serenity and perfect rest Of every pious soul--to see Thy face, The end and the beginning--One the guide, The traveller, the pathway, and the goal.
items.latin_first: O qui perpetua mundum ratione gubernas

prayer_he_wrote.note: Capitals: James prints 'By thy will' (1.5) and 'To thee their fires' (3.9) in lower case; display 'Thy' and 'Thee'. The lines chosen above already have James's capitals. The 3.9 prayer is Philosophy's, so label it 'a prayer he wrote for Philosophy to sing', not 'his prayer'.

hub_card.text: Hints confirmed: he lived about 480 to 524/526 and wrote everything after 500, so '500on'; Latin West, so 'west'. Groups: the mock-up gives none. Suggest 'martyrs': the Roman Martyrology and Pavia call him a martyr, with the caveat stated on the page. 'teachers' is also defensible (the Catholic Encyclopedia: the schoolmen 'depended entirely on Boethius' for Aristotle), but that group is for the great teachers of the Church, so leave it to the owner. Not 'fathers' (not usually counted a Church Father), not a monk, desert father or Cappadocian.
hub_card.source: Roman Martyrology via Cathopedia; Catholic Encyclopedia; mockup/src/build.mjs (boethius: groups '', '500on', 'west', focus '50% 45%')

site_data_flags.text: people.boethius.dates 'c. 477 to c. 524': fine as a middle. The checked sources give birth about 480 (CE, Stewart and Rand, Orthodox Encyclopedia) or 475-7 (SEP), and death 524 (Stewart and Rand) or 526 (SEP). 'About 480 to 524' matches most sources.

people.boethius.hook: 'Condemned without a hearing' is right (Anonymus Valesianus 87; Consolation 1.4 'unheard'). 'the Muses of self-pity' is interpretation: the text calls them 'the Muses of Poesie' dictating his laments. Acceptable as a paraphrase.

Three of the five shown quiz lines (anger, calm, effort) are Philosophy's words, not the prisoner's. The site should say 'in his Consolation, Philosophy says' or the recorder note, as Martin's page does with 'as Sulpicius recorded it'.
The learning line is cut mid-sentence and capitalised ('Examine carefully...'); the original is '...of another opinion, examine carefully...'. Fine, but the checker should compare case-insensitively.
The portrait credit 'Boethius teaching his students, 1385' is the Glasgow MS Hunter 374 initial per the fathers research; its licence on Commons was not re-checked in this pass.

tidbits.text: A geometry book under his name shows Hindu-Arabic numerals, zero and all ...
tidbits.evidence: D. E. Smith and L. C. Karpinski, The Hindu-Arabic Numerals (Boston, 1911), Project Gutenberg 22599 (fetched 2026-09-25 to sources/people/boethius/gutenberg-22599-smith-karpinski-hindu-arabic-numerals.txt). Line 1829: 'The genuineness of the arithmetic and the treatise on music is generally recognized, but the geometry, which contains the Hindu numerals with the zero, is under suspicion. There are plenty of supporters of the idea that Boethius knew the numerals and included them in this book, and on the other hand there are as many who feel that the geometry, or at least the part mentioning the numerals, is spurious.' Line 1431: the forms 'which tradition has so persistently assigned to Boethius (c. 500 A.D.)'. Line 1901: 'there is no reliable evidence that he did know them'. Put together later: Orthodox Encyclopedia, 'Boethius' (pravenc-boethius.txt line 191): the geometry ascribed to him in Migne, PL 63, 'имеет более позднее происхождение (X-XI вв.), хотя, возможно, и содержит отдельные фрагменты утерянного текста Б.' (is of later origin, 10th to 11th century, though it may contain fragments of his lost text); Catholic Encyclopedia (catholic-encyclopedia-boethius.txt): 'considered to be a ninth- or tenth-century elaboration of a work of Boethius. How far the work is genuine ... on the answer to this question depends the determination of the date of the first use of Arabic numerals in Western Europe.'

tidbits.text: Chaucer put his prison book into English, and so did Queen Elizabeth I. An Old English version is older still ...
tidbits.evidence: W. J. Sedgefield, King Alfred's Version of the Consolations of Boethius, done into modern English (Oxford, 1900), archive.org KingAlfredsfBoethius (Public Domain Mark), fetched 2026-09-25 to sources/people/boethius/archive-sedgefield-1900-king-alfreds-boethius.txt. Line 596: 'In England no less a poet than Geoffrey Chaucer made a prose translation. He was followed by nearly a dozen others in the following centuries, including Queen Elizabeth'. The Old English version's own prose preface, in Sedgefield's English, line 2726: 'King Alfred was the interpreter of this book, and turned it from book Latin into English'. Also Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (sep-boethius.txt line 951): 'Chaucer, who translated it into Middle English'.
tidbits.checker: Rewritten 2026-09-25 by the checker. The builder's 'King Alfred the Great put his prison book into Old English, adding thoughts of his own on a king's duty' stated Alfred's authorship in our own voice, from Cooper (1902) and the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907). Modern scholarship doubts it: Wikipedia, 'Old English Boethius' (checked 2026-09-25): 'The translation is attributed in one manuscript to King Alfred (r. 870-899), and this was long accepted, but the attribution is now considered doubtful.' The line now reports what the preface says, which is true either way, and drops the 'thoughts of his own' that hang on his authorship.

tidbits.text: He taught that music comes in three kinds ...
tidbits.evidence: Orthodox Encyclopedia, 'Boethius' (pravenc-boethius.txt line 300): 'Б. пишет о 3 родах музыки - мировой (mundana - гармония космоса), человеческой (humana - гармония человеческого естества) и издаваемой к.-л. инструментами (in quibusdam constituta instrumentis; I 2).' In English: he writes of three kinds of music, of the world (the harmony of the cosmos), human (the harmony of human nature), and that made by instruments (De institutione musica 1.2).
tidbits.checker: 'the harmony of the heavens' became 'the harmony of the universe' (2026-09-25, the checker): the Orthodox Encyclopedia's gloss is 'гармония космоса' (the harmony of the cosmos), and Boethius's musica mundana takes in the elements and the seasons as well as the heavens.

tidbits.text: He took up a question the medieval schools argued over for centuries ...
tidbits.evidence: Orthodox Encyclopedia, 'Boethius' (pravenc-boethius.txt line 235): the problem of universals, 'оказавшейся впосл. фундаментальной философско-богословской проблемой' (which later proved a fundamental philosophical and theological problem): 'имеют ли роды и виды (общие понятия, универсалии) самостоятельное бытие или же образуются разумом' (whether genera and species have their own being or are formed by the mind); his conclusion that 'универсалии существуют в телесных и чувственно воспринимаемых вещах, но постигаются отдельно от чувственного' (universals exist in bodily and sensible things, but are grasped apart from the sensible), Comm. in Porphyr. I; he 'фактически только намечает проблему буд. споров реалистов и номиналистов' (only sketches the problem of the later disputes of realists and nominalists). Porphyry raised the question and declined it: SEP (sep-boethius.txt line 213). 'Took up', not 'asked', for that reason.
tidbits.checker: The last sentence changed 2026-09-25 by the checker from 'His answer: they exist in things, and the mind grasps them apart.' to 'His answer, following Aristotle: they exist in things, and the mind draws them out.' The Orthodox Encyclopedia (pravenc-boethius.txt line 235) says he concludes it relying on Aristotle's theory of generalising by abstraction, and following Aristotle and Porphyry in his conclusion; the mind singles out the common features of things. SEP (sep-boethius.txt lines 230 to 260) describes the same answer as abstraction. 'Following Aristotle' keeps the line from presenting it as a settled view of his own. 'Apart' alone left the sentence unfinished.
